title: Ivermectin in Tropical Medicine
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Ivermectin is a broad‑spectrum anti‑helminthic used for onchocerciasis, strongyloidiasis, scabies and as part of mass drug administration for filariasis. It acts by binding glutamate‑gated chloride channels, causing paralysis of parasites.

sections.p: Ivermectin is a semi‑synthetic macrocyclic lactone derived from Streptomyces avermitilis. It is the drug of choice for several neglected tropical diseases common in East Africa.

The parasites targeted by ivermectin are mainly nematodes (e.g., Onchocerca volvulus, Strongyloides stercoralis) and ectoparasites (Sarcoptes scabiei). They rely on glutamate‑gated chloride channels for neuromuscular transmission.
Onchocerca is transmitted by blackfly bites; larvae migrate to skin and eyes. Strongyloides larvae penetrate skin, migrate to lungs, then gut. Scabies mites live in epidermis.
b: Skin penetration by Strongyloides larvae → autoinfection

sections.p: Ivermectin is used to treat river blindness (onchocerciasis), strongyloidiasis, scabies, and as part of mass drug administration for lymphatic filariasis.
b: Strongyloides: abdominal pain, eosinophilia, hyperinfection in immunosuppressed

sections.p: Clinical history and examination guide diagnosis; confirmatory tests are limited in low‑resource settings.

t.b: Positive → treat with ivermectin; negative does not rule out early disease
High eosinophils + abdominal pain → suspect strongyloides
Positive supports diagnosis but cannot quantify load

sections.p: Ivermectin is the cornerstone of treatment and control programmes. Dosage is weight‑based; monitoring for adverse effects is essential.
b: Onchocerciasis: 200 µg/kg single dose; repeat annually for 4–6 years in endemic areas
Strongyloides: 200 µg/kg twice daily for 2 days or single dose
Scabies: 200 µg/kg single dose or topical 5% permethrin

t.b: If severe, stop drug and treat supportive care

sections.p: Remember that ivermectin is contraindicated in loiasis with high microfilarial load due to risk of encephalopathy. In mass drug administration, combine with albendazole for filariasis control.
b: Avoid ivermectin in Loa loa high‑load cases

whenToSeekHelp: Severe neurological symptoms after ivermectin (encephalopathy), severe rash or anaphylaxis, persistent visual loss in onchocerciasis

faq.q: Why is ivermectin preferred over albendazole for strongyloidiasis?
faq.a: Ivermectin kills both larvae and adult worms and prevents autoinfection, whereas albendazole is less effective against larvae.

faq.q: Can ivermectin be used in pregnancy?
faq.a: It is category C; use only if benefits outweigh risks, usually avoided in first trimester.

faq.q: What is the main adverse effect of ivermectin?
faq.a: Skin rash and pruritus; severe reactions are rare but can occur with high parasite loads.

exam: 1. A 35‑year‑old man from a riverine community presents with painless visual loss and skin nodules. What is the first-line treatment? — Ivermectin 200 µg/kg single dose, repeat annually for 4–6 years. 2. A patient with strongyloidiasis is on steroids. What complication must you anticipate? — Hyperinfection syndrome; treat with high‑dose ivermectin. 3.
